why.noIdentityFieldHere: The SAN this policy demands is DERIVED from repository + workflow.path + workflow.ref by expectedCertificateIdentity() in scripts/keyless-identity.mjs, and is deliberately not also written out here. A second copy of a derived string is a second thing to keep in step, and the one that drifts is always the one a human reads.
why.identity: A keyless signature verifies against SOME Fulcio certificate, and Fulcio issues one to anybody's GitHub Actions job. This file is what turns that into provenance: the verifier demands this exact SAN and this exact issuer, so a signature made by any other workflow, repository or ref is refused. scripts/supply-chain/keyless-provenance.mjs holds this file and the workflow it names to the same answer, in both directions.
why.repository: null, and deliberately so: this repository has no git remote, so no committed file knows its GitHub owner. Inventing one would produce a policy that accepts nothing while reading as though somebody had reviewed it. Until an owner is committed here, the owner is resolved from GITHUB_REPOSITORY (bounded by repositoryName above) for the workflow's verification of its own signature, and security:image-provenance REFUSES a committed keyless record that needed that fallback — an outsider checking this repository has no environment to resolve.
why.exactNotRegexp: cosign offers --certificate-identity-regexp and this policy does not use it. An unanchored pattern matches a longer string, and a wildcard in the ref accepts a signature made from any branch. The signing workflow is workflow_run-triggered, which GitHub always runs on the default branch, so exactly one ref is reachable and an exact string expresses it.
why.transparencyLog: Required. Keyless signing without Rekor throws away the property that makes it worth the exercise: without a public record that the certificate was issued at a time, a compromise is not detectable after the fact, which is the residual the key-based posture is stuck with.
